content: Ear pain, also known as otalgia, can originate either from within the ear itself or from structures outside the ear. Determining the exact cause of otalgia can be challenging due to the complex innervation of the ear. Sensory input to the middle ear, external auditory canal, auricle, and peri-auricular tissues is provided by branches of the fifth (trigeminal), seventh (facial), ninth (glossopharyngeal), and tenth (vagus) cranial nerves, as well as cervical nerves C1, C2, and C3. Interestingly, otalgia can sometimes be a manifestation of myocardial ischemia (such as an angina equivalent), as the vagus nerve provides sensory innervation to both the heart and the ear. Otalgia is classified into two categories: primary otalgia, which originates from the ear, and secondary otalgia, which originates from structures outside the ear. When the ear examination reveals abnormalities, the pain is likely primary otalgia. Conversely, if the ear examination is normal, the pain is more likely secondary otalgia. A thorough examination should include inspection of the nasal cavity, oral cavity, neck, and potentially the larynx to identify the source of the pain. Life-Threatening Causes While otalgia itself is not life-threatening, certain characteristics may indicate a more serious underlying condition. Patients over the age of 50, those with coronary artery disease, diabetes, or immunocompromised states, as well as individuals who smoke, consume alcohol, or experience unintentional weight loss, should be evaluated more carefully. Otalgia may also be the first presenting symptom of serious conditions such as: Temporal arteritis Myocardial infarction Thoracic aneurysms Subdural hematoma Lung cancer Carotid artery aneurysm Pott puffy tumor Malignant neoplasms Common Causes Primary Otalgia Common causes of primary otalgia include: Otitis media Otitis externa Barotrauma Eustachian tube dysfunction Presence of a foreign object in the ear Cellulitis of the auricle Cholesteatoma Secondary Otalgia Common causes of secondary otalgia include: Bell’s palsy Carotidynia Cervical adenopathy Cervical spine arthritis Cricoarytenoid arthritis Dental infections Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) Head and neck tumors Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) syndrome Myofascial pain Neuralgias (trigeminal, glossopharyngeal, geniculate, sphenopalatine) Oral aphthous ulcers Pharyngitis or tonsillitis Salivary gland disorders Sinusitis Thyroiditis Diagnosis An algorithm summarizing the diagnostic approach to ear pain, as outlined in the American Family Physician (AFP) 2008 guidelines, should be followed to systematically evaluate the patient and identify the underlying cause. Treatment Similarly, treatment of ear pain should follow the algorithm provided in the American Family Physician guidelines, ensuring evidence-based management tailored to the specific etiology of the otalgia.
